panelists.name: panelist-1
panelists.rationale: Basis is the dataset's MAGNA media-owner-revenue series, where 2024 is $380bn and 2025 is $398bn; on eMarketer's wider definition the same year reads about $422bn, so the level is basis-dependent and the growth rate is the real forecast. The outside view comes from advertising as a share of nominal GDP: 1.17% in 2021, 1.25% in 2022, 1.22% in 2023, 1.30% in 2024 and 1.29% in 2025 against BEA nominal GDP of $29.298trn and $30.762trn. Two regularities do the work. Since 2018 the ratio has drifted up about 0.16pp, an elasticity to nominal GDP near 1.35, which is the post-2019 structural break; and cyclical years add a further 0.07 to 0.08pp (2022 added 0.076, 2024 added 0.078). Applying a 0.064pp cyclical step to 1.294% gives 1.358% of a 2026 nominal GDP of roughly $32.1trn, or $436bn. A structural build agrees: traditional media owners hold near $104bn as roughly $6.5bn of secular decline is offset by about $5.5bn of net incremental linear political money (AdImpact projects a record $11.6bn cycle, $5.6bn broadcast and $1.4bn cable) plus about $1.5bn from the Milan-Cortina Olympics and the World Cup, leaving digital near $332bn. The forecaster panel brackets this: Dentsu at +5.0% to $415bn (Dec 2025), MAGNA at +7.8% (Jun 2025), IAB's buy-side Outlook at +9.5% (Jan 2026) and WPP Media at +11.9% (Jun 2026). Vintage-weighting toward the newer reads gives +9.5%. Q1 2026 platform actuals (Meta +33%, Amazon +24%, Google +16%) argue for more, but those are global and I discounted them for recency bias, pulling my bottom-up of $443bn down. The interval is deliberately wider than the analyst spread because the $398bn base is an in-year estimate, not a closed actual, and MAGNA has already changed its published taxonomy once.
panelists.reference_class: Long-run US advertising-to-nominal-GDP (Coen/MAGNA/IRS rails, 1919-2025), with the post-2019 elasticity break and the observed cyclical-year step of +0.07 to +0.08pp in 2022 and 2024

panelists.name: panelist-2
panelists.rationale: Anchored on the dataset's own basis: 2024 = $380B, 2025 = $398B as MAGNA's June-2025 in-year estimate, reconciled by era-7 to a $405B central with CI80 [390, 425]. IAB subsequently reported 2025 US growth at +5.7%, implying a final near $402-405B, so I take $403B as the 2025 working actual. The mid-year 2026 forecaster spread is wide: Dentsu +5.0%, WARC +7%, MAGNA's stale first look +7.8%, IAB Outlook +9.5%, and WPP Media's June-2026 midyear +11.9% after an upgrade. Weighting the post-Q1 vintages at half gives +10.0%. A bottom-up build agrees: digital at +15% on a Q1 run rate where Google ads grew 16%, Meta 33% and Amazon 24%, plus traditional at roughly -3% after the ~$9B of incremental midterm, Winter Olympics and World Cup money offsets an -8% secular slide, sums to $444-448B. The reference class then adds a small upward tilt, because mid-year vintages in expansion years land 1-2% below the final actual, and I subtract a haircut for recency bias off one blowout quarter. The interval is wider than the 1-2% historical mid-year error because the dominant risk is not forecasting error but basis: eMarketer's broader definition puts 2026 above $485B, and a resolution on that series rather than the MAGNA/era basis would sit far outside a purely statistical band.
panelists.reference_class: Mid-year-vintage professional forecasts of US total ad spend versus final actual, 2019-2025 (MAGNA, GroupM/WPP Media, eMarketer, WARC, Dentsu, IAB): median absolute level error 1-2%, systematically low in expansion years, 8-10% misses in shock years (2009, 2020).

panelists.name: panelist-3
panelists.rationale: Basis is the dataset spine: MAGNA US media-owner ad revenue, where 2024 is $380B and 2025 is $398B. I built 2026 bottom-up from platform run-rates rather than from any single published forecast. Q1 2026 actuals reported before the freeze were Alphabet Google advertising $77.25B (+15.5%, with Search & other $60.4B at +19%), Meta advertising $55.02B (+33%, impressions +19% and price per ad +12%), and Amazon advertising services $17.24B (+24%). Weighting those against a residual bucket of TikTok, Microsoft, second-tier retail media networks, CTV and open-web publishers at roughly +10%, the share-weighted US digital run-rate for Q1 is about +18.6%. Decelerating each line for the stiffening comps that arrive in Q3 and Q4 (2025 growth accelerated through the year at all three platforms, so Q1 2026 faced the easiest comparison of the four) gives full-year digital growth near +14 to +16%, or roughly $336B. The traditional half starts at $104B, sheds about 5% secularly (PwC put 2025 US TV advertising at -13.4%), and regains roughly $7.2B of cyclical money: about $7.0B of AdImpact's projected $11.6B 2026 cycle lands on broadcast and cable, plus the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics and a US-hosted FIFA World Cup. Net traditional is roughly flat at $104B. That sums to $440B, or +10.6%. I then reconciled against the published anchors, weighting my structural build 60% and the forecaster consensus 40%. MAGNA's +7.8% and the IAB Outlook Study's +9.5% (28 Jan 2026, 200+ buyers) both predate the Q1 prints; WPP Media's midyear forecast published 16 June 2026, the only fully post-Q1 anchor inside the freeze, upgraded US growth by 4.5 points to +11.9%. My central sits between the pre-Q1 consensus and the post-Q1 upgrade, shaded down from the pure run-rate build because the marginal buyer driving the surge is the AI-native advertiser cohort, which is the cohort most exposed to a funding tightening. The 80% interval spans +6.0% to +16.6% growth. The low end requires a recession or an H2 deflation of AI-native demand; the high end requires the platform surge to carry unbroken and allows for a resolver using eMarketer's larger US total (roughly $422B in 2025).
panelists.reference_class: Platform revenue run-rates: share-weighted Q1 2026 US ad revenue growth of Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and the residual seller base, decelerated for comp stiffening and grossed up to the MAGNA media-owner total by adding a separately modelled traditional-media half.

forecasts.spread_note: The gap is about which 2025 base and which forecast vintage to trust rather than about the market itself: panelist-1 anchors an ad-to-nominal-GDP outside view on the unrevised $398bn MAGNA base and explicitly discounts the Q1 2026 platform prints as global and recency-biased, while panelist-2 and panelist-3 start from a reconciled ~$403-405bn base and weight the post-Q1 evidence (WPP Media's +11.9% June upgrade, share-weighted platform run-rates near +18.6%) far more heavily.

forecasts.target: Full-year 2026 US digital share of total ad spend

panelists.name: panelist-1
panelists.rationale: Defined as IAB/PwC internet revenue divided by the MAGNA US total, which is the natural construction from the two stitch series in adspend.json. That gives 68.0% for 2024 ($258.571bn of $380bn) and 74.0% for 2025 ($294.593bn of $398bn). The 6pp single-year jump is partly real and partly a MAGNA vintage artifact; the dataset's concordance note confirms the two series agree to within 0.2% in 2025 but offers no such check for 2024, so I treat 74.0% as the reliable anchor and the 2024 reading as soft. For 2026 the share arithmetic is disciplined by the level forecast: digital near $332bn on $294.593bn (+12.7%) against traditional near $104bn (roughly flat), giving 76.2%. The gain of 2.2pp is smaller than 2025's because a midterm plus Winter Olympics plus World Cup year is precisely when linear television stops falling; AdImpact's projected $7.0bn of broadcast and cable political money is the single largest support traditional media has had since 2024. The pull in the other direction is that political dollars increasingly route to connected TV and digital ($2.6bn CTV and $1.68bn digital in AdImpact's cycle projection), which lands in the digital numerator on the IAB basis. IAB's own May 2026 component forecasts have digital video decelerating to +11% and social video to +13%, well below 2025 actuals, which caps the share gain. The interval is narrow relative to the level forecast because numerator and denominator move together and definitional shifts partly cancel; the residual width is basis risk, principally another MAGNA DPP/TMO taxonomy change or a restatement of the 2025 traditional line.
panelists.reference_class: Annual digital share transitions in US measured media 2015-2025, with the specific sub-class of cyclical (election plus major sporting event) years in which linear TV growth temporarily compresses the share gain

panelists.name: panelist-2
panelists.rationale: The dataset's era-7 claim puts digital at roughly 72% of US total ad spend in 2025, from IAB/PwC internet revenue of $294.593B against a reconciled total near $405-409B; on MAGNA's own digital-pure-player line the 2024-to-2025 move was 70.5% to 73.9%. Share gains have run 1.5 to 3.5 points a year, and they compress in cyclical years because political, Olympics and World Cup money lands disproportionately in linear TV, radio and out-of-home. That base rate alone argues for about 75.0% in 2026. The structural build argues slightly higher: digital at +15% against a total at +10.2% implies 76.3%. I split the two at 75.5%. The interval is set by denominator ambiguity rather than by growth uncertainty, since numerator and denominator errors largely cancel in a ratio. If the resolver measures the total on eMarketer's broader basis while keeping IAB in the numerator, the same underlying market prints closer to 70%, which is why the lower bound sits three points below central rather than the one point a pure growth-error band would justify.
panelists.reference_class: Annual change in US digital share of total ad spend, 2015-2025, on matched IAB/PwC numerator and MAGNA-basis denominator, split into cyclical (even) and non-cyclical (odd) years; share gains of 1.5-3.5 points per year, damped in political/Olympic years.

panelists.name: panelist-3
panelists.rationale: Basis is IAB/PwC US internet ad revenue divided by the MAGNA US total, which is how the dataset is constructed and which is internally coherent because MAGNA's own 2025 digital pure-player line ($294B) and IAB's 2025 total ($294.593B) are the same number to within 0.2%. On that basis the share was 66.6% in 2023, 68.0% in 2024 and 74.0% in 2025. The five-point jump into 2025 is real but flattered by arithmetic: digital grew 13.9% while the total grew only 4.6% because the 2024 base carried presidential-cycle political money on traditional media. My 2026 build puts digital at roughly $336B (+14.1%) against a total of $440B (+10.6%), which is a share near 76.4%. I set the central slightly below that at 76.0% for one structural reason. 2026 is a cyclical year, and cyclical money lands disproportionately on broadcast, cable and out-of-home. In the last comparable cyclical year, 2024, the digital share advanced only 1.4 points. AdImpact's cycle projection of $11.6B puts roughly $7.0B on broadcast and cable against $2.6B on connected TV and $1.68B on digital, so the political mix in 2026 is unusually traditional-weighted for a modern cycle. A share gain of 2.0 points rather than 2.4 is the more likely reading. The interval is asymmetric downward. The upper bound is arithmetically constrained because traditional media cannot collapse in a year when it is receiving political, Olympic and World Cup inflows. The lower bound carries basis risk: a resolver using eMarketer's net digital measure against eMarketer's broader total lands nearer 70%, and a resolver using MAGNA's own internally revised split could differ by a point or two. Anyone reading this number should be told which two series it divides, because the answer moves by six points depending on the answer.
panelists.reference_class: Platform revenue run-rates expressed as a ratio: IAB/PwC seller-reported US internet ad revenue, projected from Alphabet, Meta and Amazon Q1 2026 growth, divided by a MAGNA-basis total whose traditional half is modelled separately from cyclical event inflows.

forecasts.spread_note: All three divide IAB/PwC internet revenue by a MAGNA-basis total and agree the 2026 share gain is damped by cyclical money, but they start from different 2025 shares: panelist-1 and panelist-3 take 74.0% as the anchor and read AdImpact's traditional-weighted cycle ($7.0bn of $11.6bn to broadcast and cable) as capping the gain at 2.0-2.2pp, while panelist-2 works from a lower ~72% starting share on a reconciled $405bn denominator and therefore lands lower despite assuming faster digital growth.

panelists.name: panelist-1
panelists.rationale: The dataset carries no retail media series, so this target sits entirely outside adspend.json and the definitional spread is the dominant uncertainty. Three published anchors: EMARKETER's December 2025 forecast puts US retail media at $60.32bn in 2025 rising to $71.09bn in 2026 (+17.8%); the May 2026 vintage relayed through Statista revises the 2025 base down to $58.8bn and 2026 to $69.3bn (+17.9%), so the growth rate held while the base moved; and IAB/PwC's FY2025 report puts commerce media at $63.4bn (+18%), a broader cut that treats commerce as a cross-category slice of search, display and video rather than a channel. Three independent measurements converging on roughly 18% growth is a strong signal, and it is corroborated on the supply side by Amazon's Q1 2026 advertising revenue of $17bn (+24%, trailing-twelve-month above $70bn), with EMARKETER attributing 79.7% of the US retail media market to Amazon in 2025. Non-Amazon networks (Walmart Connect at 8.0% share, plus Instacart, Kroger, Roundel, DoorDash and Uber) grow faster still, and 2026 adds in-store and off-site inventory to the addressable base. I take growth slightly above the consensus 18% because the Amazon print already exceeded it, giving roughly $71bn on a base near $60bn. As a cross-check, $71bn is 21.4% of my $332bn digital estimate, almost exactly the 21.5% of digital that IAB assigned commerce media in 2025. The interval is asymmetric-wide because a commerce-media basis rather than a retail-media basis would put the same year near $75bn, and because retail media is the category most exposed to reclassification as networks fold in-store and CTV inventory into their reported numbers.
panelists.reference_class: Emerging digital ad channels in their high-growth decade (paid search 2003-2010, social 2012-2018, connected TV 2019-2024), which sustain 15-25% growth for several years past $50bn before decelerating; cross-checked against the three published US retail media forecast vintages

panelists.name: panelist-2
panelists.rationale: The dataset's 2025 anchor is $60.32B on eMarketer's retail media definition, with Amazon taking about 79.7%, against $63.4B for IAB/PwC's wider commerce media measure. eMarketer's December-2025 forecast put 2026 at $71.09B, a +17.9% rise; IAB's Outlook has commerce media at +12.1%, which on the same base is $67.6B. Two things push me above the published $71.09B. First, Amazon's advertising services grew 24% year on year in Q1 2026, well ahead of the mid-teens the December forecast assumed, and Amazon is four-fifths of the pool. Second, this specific series carries a documented one-directional revision bias: eMarketer has repeatedly restated US retail media upward as it folds in in-store and off-site inventory, once lifting a single year's forecast by more than $4B. That is a reference-class property, not a judgment call, and it is the reason the interval is skewed right. The downside case is straightforward deceleration, since annual growth has stepped down from roughly 28% to 21% to 17-18% across 2023-2025, and a return to that glide path with no restatement lands near $67B.
panelists.reference_class: eMarketer US retail media ad spending forecast vintages versus subsequent restated actuals, 2021-2025, cross-checked against IAB/PwC commerce media; growth decelerating ~3-4 points a year with a persistent upward restatement bias from definitional expansion.

panelists.name: panelist-3
panelists.rationale: Basis is eMarketer's US retail media ad spending definition, which is the basis carried in the dataset's era-7 record at $60.32B for 2025 with Amazon at 79.7% of it. Two independent paths converge tightly. Path one is the published forecast: eMarketer's H1 2026 vintage puts 2026 at $71.09B (+17.9%), and an earlier September 2025 vintage put it at $69.33B, so the compiler's own vintage spread is under $2B. Path two is the platform run-rate build, which is my assigned lens. Amazon US retail media was roughly $48.1B in 2025. Amazon's global advertising services grew 24% in Q1 2026 and crossed $70B on a trailing-twelve-month basis, but retail media proper grows slower than total Amazon advertising because Prime Video inventory and the DSP sit partly outside the retail media definition, so about +18% gives $56.8B. That lands almost exactly on eMarketer's separately published $56.71B Amazon forecast. The non-Amazon tier was about $12.2B in 2025; Walmart Connect is forecast at $5.99B for 2026, and Instacart, Kroger, Target, DoorDash and Uber are compounding in the low twenties, so roughly $15.0B. The two components sum to $71.8B. I set the central at $71.5B, a shade under the arithmetic, because eMarketer's own May 2026 report leads with the finding that retail media growth is slowing and that a scaled second tier is only now emerging. The interval is wide and right-skewed for one reason that has nothing to do with growth: definition. IAB's commerce media line was $63.4B in 2025 on the same year, roughly $3B above eMarketer's retail media, and IAB forecasts it at +12.1% for 2026, which lands at a very similar $71.1B from a different base. A resolver using a wider commerce-media definition that folds in travel, financial services and marketplace listings would land materially higher; WPP Media put global commerce and retail media at $178.2B in 2025, and a US slice of that runs $85B or more. Note also that most of Amazon's contribution is sponsored-products search inventory, so this number overlaps heavily with the search forecast and must not be added to it.
panelists.reference_class: Platform revenue run-rates: Amazon's reported advertising services growth (Q1 2026 +24%, FY2025 +22%) haircut to the retail media subset, plus a separately modelled second tier of retailer networks anchored on Walmart Connect's published trajectory.

forecasts.spread_note: All three land within $1.5bn of eMarketer's published $71.09bn, so the disagreement is narrow and entirely about how much to add for Amazon's 24% Q1 beat: panelist-2 adds the most and skews its interval right on eMarketer's documented one-directional upward restatement bias, while panelist-1 and panelist-3 hold near the published figure and instead widen their intervals for the retail-media versus commerce-media definitional gap (IAB's $63.4bn commerce line on the same 2025 year).

forecasts.target: Full-year 2026 US search advertising spend, including AI-surface ads

panelists.name: panelist-1
panelists.rationale: Basis is the IAB/PwC search line carried in adspend.json, which reads $114.2bn for 2025 (+11.0%, 38.8% of the $294.593bn internet total) and about $102.9bn for 2024. This matters: on EMARKETER's wider construction, which reclassifies retail media search into the search bucket, the comparable 2026 figure is roughly $155bn to $165bn, so the basis has to be stated or the number is meaningless. The AI-surface question resolves more cleanly than the framing suggests. EMARKETER's 2026 AI advertising forecast of $32.03bn assigns more than 80% of it to conventional search ads sitting next to AI content such as Google AI Overviews, and puts genuine chatbot advertising below $1bn in 2026; AI search ads are only 0.7% of search spend in 2025, reaching 13.6% by 2029. So AI surfaces are almost entirely inside the existing search line for 2026 rather than a separate pool, and the risk they pose this year is displacement of query volume, not of measurement. Google's Q1 2026 print (advertising revenue $77bn, +16%, search at all-time-high query volume) says that displacement has not yet bitten. Growth of 12.1% to $128bn sits modestly above 2025's 11.0%, supported by Amazon-led retail search (EMARKETER expects nearly $5bn of incremental spend into retail media search in 2026, and Google falling to 48.5% of US search spend, below half for the first time in two decades) and tempered by EMARKETER's own May 2026 read that search growth is decelerating and its share of digital is slipping. The resulting $128bn is 38.6% of my $332bn digital estimate, a two-tenths slip from 2025 that is consistent with that view. The interval's downside covers a sharper AI-driven query shift; the upside covers an IAB taxonomy change moving more commerce media into the search line.
panelists.reference_class: Paid search as a share of US internet advertising revenue on the IAB/PwC series, 1996-2025, during prior interface disruptions (mobile transition 2011-2015, voice and app-store search 2016-2019), where the format line absorbed the new surface rather than being displaced by it

panelists.name: panelist-2
panelists.rationale: On the dataset's IAB/PwC format basis, US search was $102.9B in 2024 and $114.2B in 2025, or 38.8% of internet revenue, a +11.0% year. For 2026 the evidence points to acceleration rather than the feared AI-driven collapse. Google Search and other grew 19% year on year in Q1 2026 to $60.4B, with query volume up roughly 20% on AI Overviews; the Pew finding that result clicks fall from 15% to 8% when an AI summary appears is real, but the volume effect has so far more than offset the click-rate effect, and Google states the format monetises at approximately the classic-search rate. Amazon's sponsored products, which sit inside the IAB search bucket, grew 24%. Microsoft search and advertising grew 12%. Blending those with a flat long tail gives about +15.5%, or $132B. Genuinely new AI-surface inventory adds little on its own: eMarketer's $32B US AI ad spend figure for 2026 is more than 80% traditional paid search listings shown alongside AI results and therefore already counted, with chatbot placements such as OpenAI's pilot still around $100M annualised. Implied search share of digital is 39.2%, barely above 2025's 38.8%, which is the sanity check I want. The right tail reflects basis risk, since eMarketer's wider search definition implies roughly $150B for the same year.
panelists.reference_class: IAB/PwC US search format revenue, year-on-year growth 2015-2025, conditioned on the current-year Q1 growth of Google Search & other, Amazon advertising services and Microsoft search revenue; Q1 platform growth has historically bracketed the full-year IAB search print within 2-3 points.

panelists.name: panelist-3
panelists.rationale: Basis is the IAB/PwC US internet ad revenue search format line, which the dataset carries at $114.2B for 2025 (38.8% of digital) against roughly $102.9B in 2024, so +11.0%. That line grew slower in 2025 than either of its two largest constituents (Google search +13.4% globally, Amazon advertising +22%), which tells you it carries a slow or declining tail of small engines, directory-style search and app-store inventory. For 2026 the constituents accelerate. Google Search & other grew 19% in Q1 2026, the fastest print since 2021, with queries at record highs and AI Overviews monetizing at approximately the same rate as classic search; decelerating for stiffening comps gives roughly +15.5% for the full year. Amazon retail search compounds near +18 to 20%. Microsoft and the rest add high single digits. Applying the same constituent-to-IAB relationship observed in 2025, the IAB search line accelerates about two points to +13%, which is $129.0B. The AI-surface qualifier adds very little that is genuinely new. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode inventory already sits inside reported Google Search revenue. Perplexity abandoned advertising in February 2026 after generating roughly $20k against $34M of 2024 revenue. Meta AI conversation targeting is a targeting input to social inventory, not a search surface. That leaves ChatGPT ads, live in pilot since 9 February 2026 and forecast below $1B for the year, plus fragments elsewhere, so roughly $0.9B of truly incremental new-surface money. eMarketer and WPP Media put generative search at 1.3% of total search spend in 2026, rising to 13.6% by 2029, and most of that 1.3% is already counted inside Google. Central of $129.5B implies search holds 38.5% of digital, a slight continued share loss to social and CTV, consistent with IAB's own 2026 channel forecast of social +14.6% against a total of +9.5%. The interval is wide because this is the most contested line in the set. Downside: Pew measured link clicks falling from 15% to 8% when an AI summary appears, the Mehta syndication and data-sharing remedies begin to bite, and eMarketer expects Google below 50% of US search spend for the first time in two decades. Upside: AI Mode monetizing above parity, and a resolver using eMarketer's search definition, which runs roughly $20B above IAB's on the same year.
panelists.reference_class: Platform revenue run-rates: Alphabet's reported Search & other quarterly growth (Q1 2026 +19%) plus Amazon retail search and Microsoft search, mapped onto the IAB/PwC search format line via the observed 2025 constituent-to-aggregate wedge, with AI-surface inventory sized separately as incremental.

forecasts.spread_note: The spread is a direct disagreement over how much of Google's +19% Q1 Search print carries into the full IAB/PwC search line: panelist-2 passes it through most fully at +15.5%, panelist-3 decelerates it for stiffening comps and applies the observed 2025 constituent-to-aggregate wedge at +13%, and panelist-1 discounts hardest at +12.1% on eMarketer's deceleration read and AI-driven query-displacement risk; all three agree the AI-surface qualifier is nearly inert because that inventory already sits inside reported Google search revenue, leaving under $1bn genuinely new.
